q: The viscosity of a fluid is a measure of:
o: The upward force it exerts on a body immersed in it
The pressure it exerts on the walls of its container
The frictional resistance between its layers as they slide past one another
The attraction between its molecules and a solid surface
x: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid: the resistance of one layer sliding over the next. The upward force on an immersed body is the upthrust, which belongs to Archimedes' principle.

q: A small sphere moves through a viscous fluid in streamline flow. Its speed is doubled and its radius is halved. The viscous drag on it:
x: Stokes' law F = 6πηrv makes F ∝ rv, so F changes by a factor 2 × ½ = 1: it stays the same. Taking F ∝ r² (as for terminal velocity) gives the wrong factor ½.

q: Honey flows much more easily when it is warmed. This shows that, as the temperature of a liquid rises, its viscosity:
x: Warm honey pours faster, so its resistance to flow, the viscosity, has fallen: the viscosity of a liquid decreases as its temperature rises. (For gases the change is the other way, which is the usual source of confusion.)

q: Two solid spheres of the same radius, with densities 3000 kg m⁻³ and 2000 kg m⁻³, fall through a liquid of density 1000 kg m⁻³. The ratio of their terminal velocities is:
x: With upthrust, v_t = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η, so for equal radii v_t ∝ (ρ − σ): (3000 − 1000) : (2000 − 1000) = 2 : 1. Ignoring the upthrust gives 3000 : 2000 = 3 : 2.

q: Stokes' law, F = 6πηrv, gives the drag force correctly only for:
o: A large sphere moving fast enough to cause turbulence
A body of any shape moving at any speed
A sphere held at rest in a fluid
A small sphere moving slowly through a fluid in streamline flow
x: Stokes' law is derived for a small sphere moving slowly, so that the fluid flows past it in smooth streamlines. Once the flow becomes turbulent the drag no longer rises in proportion to v, and a sphere at rest feels no viscous drag at all.

q: When the speed of a liquid flowing through a pipe is increased beyond a certain critical value, the flow becomes:
o: Steady, with streamlines fixed in place
Turbulent, with eddies and irregular paths
x: Below a critical speed the flow is laminar (streamline); above it the flow becomes turbulent, with eddies and irregular, changing paths. Speeding up a fluid does not remove its viscosity.

q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows at 3 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of cross-sectional area 4 cm². The mass of water passing any cross-section each second is:
x: Volume per second = Av = 4 × 10⁻⁴ × 3 = 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³, so mass per second = ρAv = 1000 × 1.2 × 10⁻³ = 1.2 kg. Converting 4 cm² as 4 × 10⁻² m² gives 120 kg.

q: A main water pipe of cross-sectional area 6 cm² carries water at 2 m s⁻¹. It divides into three identical branch pipes, each of cross-sectional area 1 cm². The speed of the water in each branch is:
x: Continuity for the whole flow: A₁v₁ = 3A₂v₂, so 6 × 2 = 3 × 1 × v₂ and v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹. Sending all the flow through one branch (forgetting the 3) gives 12 m s⁻¹.

q: A smooth stream of water falling from a tap becomes narrower as it falls. The reason is that:
o: Surface tension squeezes the stream more strongly as it falls
The water speeds up as it falls, so by continuity its cross-section must decrease
The density of the water increases as it falls
The air pressure on the stream increases as it falls
x: Gravity accelerates the water, and for an incompressible liquid the flow rate Av is the same at every level, so where v is larger the area A is smaller. Water is practically incompressible, so its density does not change.

q: Blood leaves the heart through the aorta, of cross-sectional area 4 cm², at an average speed of 30 cm s⁻¹. It then passes through capillaries whose total cross-sectional area is 2400 cm². The average speed of blood in the capillaries is:
x: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₂ = 4 × 30/2400 = 120/2400 = 0.05 cm s⁻¹. Multiplying by the larger area instead of dividing gives 18000 cm s⁻¹; the others are decimal slips.

q: Bernoulli's equation for a fluid in steady flow is an application of the law of conservation of:
x: Bernoulli's equation equates the work done by pressure to the changes in kinetic and potential energy per unit volume, so it is conservation of energy. Conservation of mass gives the equation of continuity instead.

q: Two boats moving fast side by side, close together and parallel, tend to be pulled towards each other. The reason is that:
o: Water flows faster between them, so the pressure there is lower than on their outer sides
Water flows slower between them, so the pressure there is lower than on their outer sides
The boats attract each other by gravitation
The waves from each boat push the other boat towards it
x: The water squeezed through the narrow gap moves faster, and by Bernoulli's principle faster flow means lower pressure. The higher pressure on the outer sides pushes the boats together. Gravitational attraction between boats is far too small to matter.

q: In Bernoulli's equation, P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant, each term has the dimensions of:
x: Each term has the unit of pressure, N m⁻² = N m/m³ = J m⁻³, which is energy per unit volume (e.g. ½ρv² is kinetic energy per unit volume). Energy per unit mass would need each term divided by ρ.

q: Water (density 1000 kg m⁻³) flows through a horizontal pipe whose wide part has four times the cross-sectional area of its narrow part. The speed in the wide part is 1 m s⁻¹. The pressure in the wide part exceeds that in the narrow part by:
x: Continuity gives v₂ = 4 × 1 = 4 m s⁻¹. Bernoulli: P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ × 1000 × (16 − 1) = 7500 Pa. Forgetting the ½ gives 15000 Pa; ignoring v₁ gives 8000 Pa; not squaring the speeds gives 1500 Pa.

q: A body floats at rest, partly submerged in a liquid. The upthrust on it is:
x: The body is in equilibrium, so the upward upthrust balances its weight exactly (law of flotation). If the upthrust were greater it would rise; if less it would sink.

q: A ship sails from a fresh-water river into the sea, where the water is denser. Its load is unchanged. The ship:
o: Sinks a little, because sea water is denser
Floats at exactly the same level, because its weight has not changed
Rises a little, because a smaller volume of the denser water gives the same upthrust
Rises a little, because the upthrust in sea water becomes greater than its weight
x: Floating, upthrust = weight in both waters. Upthrust = ρVg, so with a larger ρ a smaller submerged volume V is needed: the ship rises a little. At rest the upthrust still equals the weight, not more.

q: A solid loses 2.0 N of its weight when completely immersed in water (density 1000 kg m⁻³), and 1.6 N when completely immersed in an oil. The density of the oil is:
x: The loss of weight is the upthrust ρVg, and V is the same in both liquids, so ρ_oil/ρ_water = 1.6/2.0 and ρ_oil = 0.8 × 1000 = 800 kg m⁻³. Inverting the ratio gives 1250 kg m⁻³.

q: A balloon holds 10 m³ of helium (density 0.2 kg m⁻³) in air of density 1.3 kg m⁻³. Ignoring the mass of the balloon fabric, the largest load it can hold up is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Upthrust = 1.3 × 10 × 10 = 130 N; weight of helium = 0.2 × 10 × 10 = 20 N; spare lift = 110 N, which supports a mass of 110/10 = 11 kg. Ignoring the helium's weight gives 13 kg; giving the 110 N as kg gives 110 kg.
